To All,

I want to use principle component scores of habitat variables as coviariates
in my analysis. I was getting strange looking plots of the detection
functions that include the covariates. Can program distance run
analyses with negative values for covariates?

My attempt at a fix....I created a new project and shifted the PC scores
to positive values by adding the absolute value of the minimum score to all
values. The analysis then ran very smoothly and the plots looked presumeably
like they should have. For the purposes of use as a covariate, I'm not
really concerned with the sign of the relationship. I'm interested in the
magnitude of the difference. So...Is this shifting the range of my covariate
a viable approach or is it nonsense? Or is there an altoghther different
problem? I really appreciate the help. Thanks.

Jared Zimmerman
Georgia Southern University

messages.body_plain:
Distance Samplers:

This is probably perfectly obvious, but this old dog is having trouble
learning the new tricks. I thought that specifying multiple detection
functions within the CDS analysis engine via the 'Models' tab (with, e.g.,
AIC as the selector) would yield a model average point estimate as well as
variances as estimated using the bootstrapping. I'm getting no end of error
messages from the bootstrapping, and although I do, in the end, get
bootstrapped variance estimates for some (not all) of the selected models,
the remainder of the output is identical to that of the top model (as
determined in a separate, stand-alone) run. In one-at-a-time runs,
reasonable detection functions all have similar AIC, log-likelihood, and GOF
properties, but return rather different estimates of density, thus my
discomfort with using only the top model. Sample size is, alas, small (32
total animal groups, 30 after 5% truncation, 29 after 10%), and this may be
the root of the problem. Alas, the animals are in Mongolia and this survey
is not easily replicated - the sample size is what it is! (Also aggravating
is that all binning and truncation strategies tend to lead, naively, toward
the negative exponential, which I'm uncomfortable relying on, so am
tentatively rejecting it despite it AIC-appeal!).

Any clues to where I'm going wrong?

Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
Rich-

Distance does not have any model averaging capability at present but you
can include model uncertainty in the variance estimate by running each
model in each bootstrap and having it select the best model for each
bootstrap run.  To do this you put each model specification in the
analysis specification and tell it to select based on min aic.  Now the
only oddity in all that is you are still left with using the point
estimate from the best model unless you want to take the average density
across all the bootstrap runs.

But given the problems you are having with the bootstrap with the small
number of observations, I suggest you take the estimates and variances
from your various models and construct the model averaged estimate and
its variance.  It is quite easy to do and probably should be included in
Distance (what say you Len?).  Note that when you compute the variance
for the model averaged estimate, don't use the formula 4.9 in B&A model
selection.  Instead use 6.12 on page 345 of the second edition.

--jeff

messages.subject_clean: Model-averaging across detection functions with similar
messages.body_plain:
Newer versions of Distance do actually have a model averaging capability
- the Bootstrap Summary section reports the mean of the bootstrap
estimates (under estimate), which should be different from the point
estimate for any particular model.

For those who don't know how to set it up in Distance, here's how.  Say
you have found that the half-normal with cosine adjustments and the
hazard rate with simple polynomials both have similar AICs but produce
quite different abundance estimates (see below for more on when this
happens).  You want to obtain a model-averaged estimate of abundance,
plus confidence limits that reflect uncertainty as to which model is
best.  To do this, set up a new analysis, and create a new model
definition.  In the Detection Function | Models tab of the model
definition, click the plus button and you'll now be able to set 2 models
up: hn+cos and hr+poly.  The default option is to select among them
using AIC, so that's probably fine for what you want.  Under Detection
Function | Adjustment terms you probably want automatic.  Now go to the
Variance tab, and click the option to do a bootstrap (start with say 10
and if this works do another run with 999 or 1000 or some such).  Now
run it.  Each bootstrap rep, it will select adjustment terms for each of
the two models in turn, and then choose the best model using AIC.
Results in the Bootstrap Summary section will be model averaged, as
described above.

If you want to find out what proportion of times different models were
selected, you can save the bootstrap statistics file and look in there.

You said you get errors.  It's important to understand what's causing
them and fix it, if possible.
- One thing that happens with small sample sizes is that the models
don't converge properly with too many adjstment terms (resulting in
errors), so the best thing to do is to stop it fitting more than, say, 2
parameters (or 3) in total -- under Detection Function | Adjustment
terms, set Maximum terms to 2 or 3.
- You mention binning.  Only do this to exact data if you have some
problem in the data.  If you have a problem in the data (such as
rounding to 0 distance) combined with small sample size then you really
are in trouble!  Pehaps you could stick with fitting really simple,
robust models (hn + up to 1 cos adj; unif + up to 2 cos or poly adj;
perhaps hazard rate) and leave it at that.
- Don't use the negative exponential.  It's only a realistic model if
g(0)<1, and if this is the case you're in trouble anyway!
- When you have spiked data, the hazard rate shape parameter can head
down to 1, causing an unstable fit.  I've forgotten if there is a lower
bound on this parameter already, but if not you could set one (of 1)
under detection function | Constraints.
- The fact that you get very different estimates of p but similar AIC
with different models indicates that you have a small sample size,
and/or data that does not show a wide shoulder.  With "good" data,
models with similar AICs give similar p's.

Jeff suggested manual model averaging, and rightly pointed out it's easy
to do.  I agree it would be easy to add to Distance -- but bootstrapping
makes fewer assumptions and I haven't come across a case yet where it
didn't work (but maybe this is the first!)...

Lastly, I'm coauthor on a recent paper where we used model averaging to
increase the robustness of a line transect analysis (for killer whales)
-- our sample size was 18!  May have some other useful tips.  The paper is
Williams, R. and L. Thomas. 2009. Cost-effective abundance estimation of
rare animals: Testing performance of small-boat surveys for killer
whales in British Columbia. Biological Conservation 142: 1542-1547
and a copy is available at
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/papers/WilliamsBiolCons2009.pdf

Hope this helps,

  - Len

--

messages.body_plain:
Dear Colleagues,

thanks for the details and relevant question.

I am amazed to see these efforts below (manual or bootstrap-based model
averaging); and here why:

The problem of averaging across somewhat parsimonious models
is not so new.

But the lesson from these efforts, in  my mind, is that it does not work
so well (it has been shown in AIC model averaging etc. Just try it out in
your own data and check for 'generalization' accuracy when findings are
applied elsewhere. This makes for an interesting research subject).

You see that problem specifically when such models get applied on a larger
scale, and in predictions, or for wider density and population estimates.

The assumption that a 'good parsimonious fit' results automatically into a
good/"robust" application and generalization + prediction is not well
founded.

One way around it could be to use a different, non-parsimonious and
non-linear statistical framework.
'Machine Learning' (e.g. Breiman 2001) is one of those, and it's widely
applied in statistical applications elsewhere (e.g. industrial, medical,
pharmaceutical, engineering, online), and with good success.

The use of Ensemble Models might offer other options (that might be the best
approach when dealing with several fit algorithms).

There is another big advantage in such methods in that they can be
automatized fairly well; not much human decision-making is involved to
obtain 'optimal' results then.

So I wonder if there are any thoughts to apply such concepts in DS and its
software, too ? At least for the R-versions, that should be rel. easy to do.

My interest here is to obtain the best possible detection curve, density
value, and population estimate eventually. Again, I do not believe that
traditional model averaging can achieve that so well. Time, required skill
and convenience are factors to consider, too, e.g. for in-time conservation
decisions.

>From that, I feel that the times of strict linear, parsimonious approaches,
and ones that are traditionally inference-based, are somewhat over.
If that is true, much of our earlier DS derived population estimates might
have to be re-assessed then.

This is open for more testing obviously, and I wish to learn on such
research. There are many reasons though why the promotion of "Occam's Razor"

cannot work well in complex ecological studies.

I would welcome any thoughts and discussions, and specifically for the
specific DS and population prediction context. Thanks in advance.

Very best

      F.

Subject: Re: [DIST-SAMP] Model-averaging across detection functions with
similar AIC/model fit characteristics

Newer versions of Distance do actually have a model averaging capability
- the Bootstrap Summary section reports the mean of the bootstrap
estimates (under estimate), which should be different from the point
estimate for any particular model.

For those who don't know how to set it up in Distance, here's how.  Say
you have found that the half-normal with cosine adjustments and the
hazard rate with simple polynomials both have similar AICs but produce
quite different abundance estimates (see below for more on when this
happens).  You want to obtain a model-averaged estimate of abundance,
plus confidence limits that reflect uncertainty as to which model is
best.  To do this, set up a new analysis, and create a new model
definition.  In the Detection Function | Models tab of the model
definition, click the plus button and you'll now be able to set 2 models
up: hn+cos and hr+poly.  The default option is to select among them
using AIC, so that's probably fine for what you want.  Under Detection
Function | Adjustment terms you probably want automatic.  Now go to the
Variance tab, and click the option to do a bootstrap (start with say 10
and if this works do another run with 999 or 1000 or some such).  Now
run it.  Each bootstrap rep, it will select adjustment terms for each of
the two models in turn, and then choose the best model using AIC.
Results in the Bootstrap Summary section will be model averaged, as
described above.

If you want to find out what proportion of times different models were
selected, you can save the bootstrap statistics file and look in there.

You said you get errors.  It's important to understand what's causing
them and fix it, if possible.
- One thing that happens with small sample sizes is that the models
don't converge properly with too many adjstment terms (resulting in
errors), so the best thing to do is to stop it fitting more than, say, 2
parameters (or 3) in total -- under Detection Function | Adjustment
terms, set Maximum terms to 2 or 3.
- You mention binning.  Only do this to exact data if you have some
problem in the data.  If you have a problem in the data (such as
rounding to 0 distance) combined with small sample size then you really
are in trouble!  Pehaps you could stick with fitting really simple,
robust models (hn + up to 1 cos adj; unif + up to 2 cos or poly adj;
perhaps hazard rate) and leave it at that.
- Don't use the negative exponential.  It's only a realistic model if
g(0)<1, and if this is the case you're in trouble anyway!
- When you have spiked data, the hazard rate shape parameter can head
down to 1, causing an unstable fit.  I've forgotten if there is a lower
bound on this parameter already, but if not you could set one (of 1)
under detection function | Constraints.
- The fact that you get very different estimates of p but similar AIC
with different models indicates that you have a small sample size,
and/or data that does not show a wide shoulder.  With "good" data,
models with similar AICs give similar p's.

Jeff suggested manual model averaging, and rightly pointed out it's easy
to do.  I agree it would be easy to add to Distance -- but bootstrapping
makes fewer assumptions and I haven't come across a case yet where it
didn't work (but maybe this is the first!)...

Lastly, I'm coauthor on a recent paper where we used model averaging to
increase the robustness of a line transect analysis (for killer whales)
-- our sample size was 18!  May have some other useful tips.  The paper is
Williams, R. and L. Thomas. 2009. Cost-effective abundance estimation of
rare animals: Testing performance of small-boat surveys for killer
whales in British Columbia. Biological Conservation 142: 1542-1547
and a copy is available at
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/papers/WilliamsBiolCons2009.pdf

Hope this helps,

messages.body_plain:
Dear Colleagues,

thanks for the details and relevant question.

I am amazed to see these efforts below (manual or bootstrap-based model
averaging); and here why:

The problem of averaging across somewhat parsimonious models
is not so new.

But the lesson from these efforts, in  my mind, is that it does not work
so well (it has been shown in AIC model averaging etc. Just try it out in
your own data and check for 'generalization' accuracy when findings are
applied elsewhere. This makes for an interesting research subject).

You see that problem specifically when such models get applied on a larger
scale, and in predictions, or for wider density and population estimates.

The assumption that a 'good parsimonious fit' results automatically into a
good/"robust" application and generalization + prediction is not well
founded.

One way around it could be to use a different, non-parsimonious and
non-linear statistical framework.
'Machine Learning' (e.g. Breiman 2001) is one of those, and it's widely
applied in statistical applications elsewhere (e.g. industrial, medical,
pharmaceutical, engineering, online), and with good success.

The use of Ensemble Models might offer other options (that might be the best
approach when dealing with several fit algorithms).

There is another big advantage in such methods in that they can be
automatized fairly well; not much human decision-making is involved to
obtain 'optimal' results then.

So I wonder if there are any thoughts to apply such concepts in DS and its
software, too ? At least for the R-versions, that should be rel. easy to do.

My interest here is to obtain the best possible detection curve, density
value, and population estimate eventually. Again, I do not believe that
traditional model averaging can achieve that so well. Time, required skill
and convenience are factors to consider, too, e.g. for in-time conservation
decisions.

>From that, I feel that the times of strict linear, parsimonious approaches,
and ones that are traditionally inference-based, are somewhat over.
If that is true, much of our earlier DS derived population estimates might
have to be re-assessed then.

This is open for more testing obviously, and I wish to learn on such
research. There are many reasons though why the promotion of "Occam's Razor"

cannot work well in complex ecological studies.

I would welcome any thoughts and discussions, and specifically for the
specific DS and population prediction context. Thanks in advance.

Very best

      F.

Hello

I would like to announce the recent publication of the following 3 papers i=
n
*NAMMCO Scientific Publications* Volume 7, North Atlantic Sightings Surveys=
:
Counting whales in the North Atlantic, 1987-2001, which may be of interest
on this list. The volume is available at www.nammco.no <http://www.nammco.no>, and pdf reprints ar=
e
available from me at kin...@gmail.com.

Gunnlaugsson, Th., V=C3=ADkingsson, G.A. and Pike, D.G. 2009. Combined
line-transect and cue-count estimate of sperm whale abundance in the North
Atlantic, from Icelandic NASS-2001 shipboard survey. NAMMCO Sci. Publ.
7:73-80.

Sperm whales (Physeter macrocephalus) pose a particular problem to shipboar=
d
surveys as they dive for extended periods and are therefore likely to be
missed (not available) even if they are right under the track line. To
address these problems the NAMMCO planning committee for the NASS 2001
survey drew up guidelines to be followed when sperm whales were sighted.
This required every deep dive to be recorded and considered to be a cue,
from which a cue-count estimate is calculated if the cue rate is known. For
those whales that did not dive before coming abeam, a conventional
line-transect estimate is calculated, which gives an instantaneous surface
estimate from which a total estimate can be obtained if the proportion of
the time spent at the surface is known. These estimates are compared and
combined. Precise dive cycle information is missing for the mostly single
all male sperm whales in this area but a preliminary estimate of 11,185 (cv
0.34) is obtained for the surveyed area with an assumed surface time of 20%
and two deep dives per hour.

Borchers, D.L., Pike, D.G., Gunnlaugsson, Th. and V=C3=ADkingsson, G.A. 200=
9.
Minke whale abundance estimation from the NASS 1987 and 2001 aerial
cue=E2=80=93counting surveys taking appropriate account of distance estimat=
ion
errors. NAMMCO Sci. Publ. 7:95-110.

We estimate the abundance of minke whales (Balaenoptera acutorostrata) from
the Icelandic coastal shelf aerial surveys carried out as part of the 1987
and 2001 North Atlantic Sightings Surveys (NASS). In the case of the 1987
survey, the probability of detecting animals at distance zero (g(0)) is ver=
y
close to 1 but there is substantial random measurement error in estimating
distances. To estimate abundance from these data, we use methods which
assume g(0)=3D1 but which include a distance measurement error model. In th=

Jeff Laake wrote:
>> >> I'm not sure I fully understand your alternative suggestion. I need to
>> >> go get B&A 2nd edition from the library (have only 1st edition on my
>> >> shelf). Won't this require having AICc model weights available? I
>> >> haven't seen anywhere in DISTANCE output that these are provided.
>> >>
> > Not sure if the model weights are output in Distance but if not they are
> > also easily calculated from the delta aic values. For each model you
> > calculate exp(-.5*delta AICc) (this is exp(0)=1 for your best model) and
> > then you normalize by dividing each by the sum across all of the models
> > you fitted and used to create the delta AICc values.

Indeed model weights are not output, but as you say they are quite easy
to do.  Personally, I don't see a strong justification for using AICc
over AIC in this case (since the former is based on a normal
approximation that is unlikely to hold for distance sampling detection
functions), but in any case if you have the recommended sample sizes of
observations it should make no difference.

Just to clarify an earlier point, in case others are contemplating this:

 > Thanks very much. Indeed, your first paragraph summarizes what I'd done,
 > and what I found.
 >
 > I re-did the bootstrap run, saving the file this time, and was able to
 > take the mean density point estimate across all thousand runs (and
 > confirmed that the models selected corresponded with their AICc rankings
 > in an approximate way). 95centiles from this output were also easily
 > obtained. I'd gotten bootstrap warnings, but no actual errors -- all the
 > data appeared to be there, as advertised. This seems to me a reasonable
 > way to proceed.

The only reason to save stuff to the bootstrap stats file is to look at
which model is selected.  The mean of the bootstrap runs, and the
95centiles are all available in the Results tab, at the end, without
having to write code read the stats file.  At least, that's what should
happen!

  - Len
